current_workflow.step: The analyst gathers the week's average Transwestern deliveries to California, San Juan lateral throughput and total East deliveries, and works out percent of capacity by hand.

The analyst collects El Paso's average deliveries to California, broken out by PG&ETop, SoCalEhr and SoCalTop, each with its capacity, deliveries and utilization percent. Capacity figures are kept up to date by hand; SoCalEhr changed from 1042 to 1250 MMBtu/d between October and December.

The analyst copies the latest posted Gas Daily prices (SoCal gas, PG&E, TW San Juan or San Juan non-Bondad, TW Permian) with their daily changes, using Thursday's prices when the report goes out on a Thursday and marking any missing points as n/a.
The analyst adds Enron Online bases (Perm-CA, SJ-CA, SJ-Waha, Perm-Waha). In late 2001 this became a one-month 'Enron basis', then 'n/a', and by February 2002 the section was dropped.

The analyst types the subject 'California Capacity Report for Week of MM/DD-MM/DD' and sends the email to the fixed Transwestern commercial distribution (Steven Harris, Kimberly Watson, Lorraine Lindberg, TK Lohman, Lindy Donoho), usually on Friday. When the week label is wrong, she sends a follow-up correction.

implementation_steps: Sit with the analyst for one report cycle to record where each number actually comes from (pipeline flow data, Gas Daily, basis quotes). The emails do not name the source systems.
Write down the current report layout as a template, using a recent email (e.g. the week of 03/11-03/15) as the reference version.
Build the capacity reference table with effective dates, seeded from the figures in recent reports, and give one owner responsibility for updating it.

Write the script so it reads one weekly input sheet (daily volumes plus Gas Daily prices), computes averages, percentages and day-over-day price changes, and renders the draft email with a subject built from the calendar.
Add range checks (utilization over 100%, week-over-week jumps, missing price points shown as n/a) and display the results with the draft.
Run the script alongside the manual report for three to four weeks and compare it figure by figure with what the analyst sends.
Switch over: the script produces the draft, and the analyst checks it and sends it to the existing distribution list.
Only if it is cheap, replace the manual input sheet with direct pulls from the flow and price sources identified in step 1.
risks: The emails do not say where the delivery and capacity data come from. If no machine-readable source exists, the script will run on a manually filled input sheet and save less time. Confirm the sources in step 1 before building any feed.
Gas Daily is a licensed publication. Pulling prices automatically may be restricted, so if needed the price table stays a manual paste into the input sheet.
A stale capacity table would quietly skew every utilization percentage. To guard against this, store an effective date for each capacity figure and flag any value not reviewed recently.

Totals made by the script could differ from the analyst's own method (for example, how she handles a short holiday week like 12/26-12/28). The parallel run catches these differences before switching over.

The value is small ($73 a month, $876 a year) and the evidence comes from one mailbox over about five active months. Spending more than a few days on this would not pay back, so keep it a script and avoid building an integration.
The report format kept changing during the period observed (the Enron basis section went away). The template has to be easy to edit, or it will go out of date.

solution.approach: A weekly script runs Friday morning (or Thursday in a short week). It takes the week's daily delivery figures for Transwestern and El Paso, a small capacity table kept under version control, and the latest posted Gas Daily prices. From these it works out the weekly averages, utilization percentages and price changes. It fills in the exact layout used in the emails today: the Transwestern paragraph, the El Paso breakdown by delivery point, the Gas Daily price table with 'n/a' for missing points, and an optional basis section. It builds the subject 'California Capacity Report for Week of MM/DD-MM/DD' from the calendar, so the week label cannot be mistyped. The output is an unsent draft addressed to the existing distribution list. The analyst checks it, adds any commentary and sends it. Sanity checks highlight values outside normal ranges, such as utilization over 100% (one week legitimately showed 103%) or a week-over-week jump, so they get a second look before sending.
components: Weekly scheduled report script (averages, utilization percentages, price changes)
Capacity reference table with effective dates, under version control
Email template that reproduces the current report layout, with the subject's week range built from the calendar
Input loader: a simple drop-in spreadsheet or CSV per week at first, replaced by direct feeds if they turn out to be available
Range checks and a missing-data list shown with the draft
Weekly CSV history of the report figures
inputs: Daily Transwestern deliveries to California, San Juan lateral throughput and East deliveries for the report week
Daily El Paso deliveries to California at PG&ETop, SoCalEhr and SoCalTop
Capacity reference table per delivery point (e.g. PG&ETop 1140, SoCalEhr 1250, SoCalTop 540 MMBtu/d), with an effective date
Posted Gas Daily prices for SoCal gas large pkgs, PG&E large pkgs, TW San Juan / San Juan (non-Bondad) and TW Permian, current and prior day
Optional Enron Online basis quotes (Perm-CA, SJ-CA, SJ-Waha, Perm-Waha)
Distribution list: steven.harris, kimberly.watson, lorraine.lindberg, tk.lohman, lindy.donoho
outputs: Draft 'California Capacity Report for Week of MM/DD-MM/DD' email in the current format, for the analyst to check and send to the Transwestern commercial team
A short list of out-of-range values and missing inputs (e.g. a price that is n/a, utilization over 100%) shown above the draft for the analyst
A weekly CSV of the computed numbers, so trends no longer have to be pieced together from old emails
solution.trigger: Weekly schedule: Friday morning, or the last business day of a short week (the evidence shows Thursday sends that use Thursday's posted Gas Daily prices).

stall_points.description: Every figure and percentage is retyped into the email each week. The process is flagged as stalled because the whole report waits on one person compiling it once a week (median gap of about 165.8 hours between sends), and nothing checks the numbers.
stall_points.quote: Transwestern's average deliveries to California were 945 MMBtu/d (87%), with San Juan lateral throughput at 865 MMBtu/d.

stall_points.description: The week date range in the subject is typed by hand. A wrong range went out to the whole distribution and needed a second correction email.
stall_points.quote: Sorry, the effective date for this new report is 01/07-01/11.

stall_points.description: Capacity numbers used to work out utilization are kept by hand and changed between reports (SoCalEhr 1042 in October, 1250 from December). A stale capacity number quietly skews every percentage.
stall_points.quote: SoCalEhr, capacity 1042 MMBtu/d, deliveries of 707 MMBtu/d (68%)

stall_points.description: This week's report was flagged as stalled. The delivery and throughput figures are typed in again from scratch rather than taken from a data feed, so each send repeats the same manual compile.
stall_points.quote: Transwestern's average deliveries to California were 1011 MMBtu/d (93%), with San Juan lateral throughput at 872 MMBtu/d.  Total East deliveries averaged 337 MMBtu/d.

stays_manual: Final review and sending, because the analyst owns the numbers that go to the commercial team and is the one who spots operational anomalies.
Commentary or context on unusual weeks, such as deliveries above 100% of capacity or sharp price moves, because that takes market judgement.
Updating the capacity table when a pipeline's posted capacity changes, because that is a business fact a person has to confirm.
Deciding which price points and basis sections to include, because the evidence shows the format changing (basis dropped, 'San Juan (non-Bondad)' replacing 'TW San Juan').
success_metric: Share of weekly California Capacity Reports sent from the generated draft without a follow-up correction email, and the analyst's minutes per report measured before and after the switch.
summary: Every week Michelle Lokay builds the California Capacity Report by hand: Transwestern and El Paso deliveries to California, capacity utilization by delivery point, Gas Daily prices with day-over-day changes, and Enron basis. She types it into an email to the same Transwestern commercial distribution list, and she has had to send a correction when the week label was wrong. A small weekly script would compute the averages and percentages, fill in the fixed email layout with the right week dates, and leave a draft for her to check and send. That removes the retyping and the arithmetic that cause errors, but the work is only worth $73 a month ($876 a year), so the build should stay small.
